title: Judicial Renaissance -- Ch. 17: Southern Cross Cement Corporation v. Philippine Cement Manufacturers Corporation: Executive Power to Protect Local Industries
keywords: Southern Cross Cement Corporation v. Philippine Cement Manufacturers Corporation

primary_topics: Chapter 17 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- CJP's account of Southern Cross Cement Corporation v. Philippine Cement Manufacturers Corporation, which clarified Republic Act 8800, the Safeguard Measures Act, and the state power to protect domestic industries from injurious import surges.

The jurisdictional holding that the Court of Tax Appeals, not the Court of Appeals, reviews every ruling of the DTI secretary 'in connection with the imposition of a safeguard measure,' including a negative one, because split jurisdiction is abhorred and the CTA holds the specialized competence.

The majority's holding that the DTI secretary may impose a general safeguard measure only upon a positive final determination by the Tariff Commission, while remaining free to disregard the Commission's recommendations and bound also to find the measure in the public interest.

CJP's Separate (Concurring and Dissenting) Opinion: he agreed on CTA jurisdiction but argued from the alter ego principle and the President's constitutional power of control that the DTI secretary may impose a safeguard measure even where the Tariff Commission has not recommended it.
sub_topics: The facts: Philcemcor's 2001 application to the DTI for a definitive safeguard measure on gray Portland cement imports, alleging declines in production, capacity utilization, market share, sales and employment, opposed by Southern Cross.
The preliminary investigation by the DTI's Bureau of Import Services and the November 7, 2001 Order imposing a provisional safeguard duty of P20.60 per 40-kilogram bag for up to 200 days.
The Tariff Commission's Formal Investigation Report of March 13, 2002 recommending that no definitive measure be imposed, the elements of serious injury not having been established.

DTI Secretary Manuel Roxas II's disagreement with that conclusion, the DOJ Opinion of Secretary Hernando Perez that Section 13 precluded his review, and his April 5, 2002 Decision denying the application while stating he had no alternative but to abide.
Philcemcor's certiorari petition to the Court of Appeals, which refused to annul the Commission's factual findings but set aside the DTI Decision and remanded the case for a final decision.

Southern Cross's Petition to the Supreme Court contending that the CA lacked jurisdiction because the remedy lay with the Court of Tax Appeals, and that the Commission's determinations bound the DTI secretary.

The DTI secretary's new Decision of June 25, 2003 imposing a definitive safeguard duty of P20.60 per bag for three years, Southern Cross's application for a TRO and its parallel CTA petition, and Philcemcor's forum-shopping motion.
The Second Division's July 8, 2004 Decision finding no malicious intent and therefore no proven forum shopping.
The jurisdictional reasoning: certiorari lies only absent a plain, speedy and adequate remedy, and Section 29 of the SMA supplies one by vesting review in the CTA within thirty days.

Three grounds for reading Section 29 to cover negative rulings: split jurisdiction is abhorred and both kinds of ruling rest on one body of facts and one set of laws; the text neither bars CTA review of a negative determination nor confers it on the CA; and an interpretation causing inconvenience and absurdity must be avoided.

The holding on the merits that Section 5 makes a positive final determination by the Tariff Commission a condition precedent, distinct from the power to impose, which belongs to the DTI secretary, who may still decline in the public interest.

The constitutional premise that the executive power to impose safeguard measures is a delegated taxing power, permitted by Section 28(2) of Article VI subject to the limitations and restrictions Congress imposes.

The distinction drawn between a 'determination' -- factual findings the Commission alone makes finally after formal investigation -- and a 'recommendation,' which nothing in the SMA obliges the secretary to adopt.

The holding that the DTI secretary cannot review the Tariff Commission's findings, the Commission being under NEDA and not a subordinate of the DTI, so that the most he may do is ignore its recommendation but not its determination.
The Court's characterization of the statutory mechanism as a check and balance between agencies with disparate specializations on a matter of national importance.

The conclusion that the CA never acquired jurisdiction, that its Decision was an absolute nullity, and that the June 25, 2003 DTI Decision drawn from it was likewise void -- the spring cannot rise higher than its source.
The referral to the Court en banc, the March 1, 2005 oral arguments before all fifteen members, and the August 2, 2005 Resolution by Justice Tinga upholding the Decision in toto by a vote of 8-5-2.

CJP's concurrence on CTA jurisdiction and on the voidness of the CA Decision, coupled with his view that the remaining purely legal issue, imbued with public interest and touching the economic security of domestic industries, should be settled once and for all.

His first argument: the power to tax belongs to Congress and may be delegated only to the President under Section 28 of Article VI, so the majority's theory of the Tariff Commission and the DTI secretary as 'agents of Congress' violates that provision.

His second and third arguments: executive power and control are vested in the President, whose control over every executive office cannot be curtailed by Congress, and the Tariff Commission as an executive agency cannot tie the Chief Executive's hands.

His fourth and fifth arguments: the DTI secretary acting as alter ego may affirm, modify or reverse the Commission's action, and the statutory limitations of Section 5 -- increased imports, serious injury and public interest -- are the real conditions, not the Commission's determination.

His sixth argument that public interest involves immeasurable variables and is indubitably a political question for an official answerable to the people rather than for a fact-finding body with no electoral mandate.

His seventh argument from contemporaneous administrative construction: Rule 13.2.a of the implementing rules, the Commission's own Order No. 00-02 describing its task as fact-finding, and TC Chairman Edgardo Abon's statement that its recommendation is only persuasive.

His rejoinder that if the secretary may reject a positive final determination, binding him to a negative one is apparently illogical, and his reading of RA 8800's purpose as protecting local industries expeditiously.

His view that the DTI secretary's Decision was properly appealable to the President, an argument the parties had not raised, and his agreement that Southern Cross's counsel deserved severe censure rather than dismissal for the untimely disclosure of the CTA petition.

The closing summary reasserting the alter ego construction, the limits on congressional restriction of presidential control, the hands-off approach to policy questions, and the leveling of the playing field.

stances.claim: The Court of Tax Appeals has jurisdiction to review the DTI secretary's ruling whether it imposes a safeguard measure or declines to, because split jurisdiction is abhorred, the same facts and laws are involved either way, and the phrase 'in connection with the imposition of a safeguard measure' encompasses the converse ruling.
stances.rhetorical_move: three-step statutory construction -- policy against split jurisdiction, plain text, and the canon against interpretations producing inconvenience and absurdity

stances.claim: The power to impose tariffs may be delegated by Congress only to the President; the majority's theory that it may be delegated to the Tariff Commission and the DTI secretary 'as agents of Congress' plainly violates Section 28(2) of Article VI.
stances.rhetorical_move: textual exclusivity argument -- the Constitution names only the President -- resolved through the alter ego principle as the sole constitutional way to uphold the secretary's power

stances.claim: The President's constitutional power of control over the entire Executive Department cannot be curtailed by Congress, so the Tariff Commission, a mere executive agency, cannot tie the Chief Executive's hands with finality, and the DTI secretary as alter ego may affirm, modify or reverse its action.
stances.rhetorical_move: syllogism from the vesting and control clauses, with statutory limitations required to conform to the fundamental law

stances.claim: Whether a safeguard measure serves the public interest is indubitably a political question for a policymaker answerable to the people, not for a fact-finding body with no electoral mandate.
stances.rhetorical_move: political-question framing based on the immeasurable and indirect variables involved and the absence of judicial parameters

stances.claim: If the DTI secretary may reject a positive final determination of the Tariff Commission, binding him to a negative determination by the same body is apparently illogical.
stances.rhetorical_move: reductio drawn from the majority's own concession that nothing in the SMA obliges the secretary to adopt the Commission's recommendations

stances.claim: Courts should adopt a hands-off approach to non-judicial concerns of government and intervene only where an act is blatantly contrary to law or the Constitution or clearly tainted with grave abuse of discretion, since there can be no meaningful economic and social progress without an effective rule of law in place.
stances.rhetorical_move: restatement of the deference doctrine, closing on the 'leveling of the playing field' axiom and the broad, life-giving strokes formula from the mining case

notable_anecdotes: The DTI secretary's April 5, 2002 Decision quoted the Tariff Commission's conclusions, recorded his disagreement with them, and then denied the application anyway on the strength of a DOJ Opinion that he had no alternative but to abide.

Despite the Petition already pending before the Supreme Court, the DTI secretary issued a new Decision on June 25, 2003 imposing the definitive P20.60 duty, prompting Southern Cross to seek a TRO while also petitioning the CTA -- and Philcemcor to accuse it of forum shopping.

CJP quotes Tariff Commission Chairman Edgardo Abon's own words at a public consultation that the Commission's recommendation 'is but recommendatory' and merely persuasive, since the law leaves public interest to the secretary's discretion.
He notes that the argument he considered decisive -- that the DTI secretary's decision was properly appealable to the President -- was never raised by the parties.
He observes that the void Court of Appeals Decision was the legal basis of the DTI's June 25, 2003 Decision, and disposes of both with the maxim that the spring cannot rise higher than its source.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 17 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reports Southern Cross Cement Corporation v. Philippine Cement Manufacturers Corporation, which clarified Republic Act 8800, the Safeguard Measures Act. Justice Panganiban traced the dispute from Philcemcor's 2001 application for a definitive safeguard measure on gray Portland cement, through the DTI's provisional P20.60 duty, to the Tariff Commission's March 2002 report finding no serious injury; DTI Secretary Manuel Roxas II disagreed with that finding but, relying on a DOJ Opinion that Section 13 barred his review, denied the application, whereupon Philcemcor obtained a Court of Appeals decision setting aside his ruling, the secretary imposed the duty anyway in June 2003, and Southern Cross pursued parallel remedies before the Supreme Court and the Court of Tax Appeals. The Second Division found no proven forum shopping and held that the CTA, not the CA, had jurisdiction, because certiorari lies only absent a plain, speedy and adequate remedy, Section 29 of the SMA supplies one, split jurisdiction is abhorred, and the phrase 'in connection with the imposition of a safeguard measure' reaches a negative ruling as well; the CA Decision was therefore an absolute nullity and the DTI Decision drawn from it void, since the spring cannot rise higher than its source. On the merits the Court held that a positive final determination by the Tariff Commission is a condition precedent to imposition, though the secretary may still decline in the public interest and is never bound to adopt the Commission's recommendations, and it described the scheme as a check and balance between agencies of disparate specializations. The en banc upheld the Decision in toto on August 2, 2005 by an 8-5-2 vote. Panganiban concurred on jurisdiction but dissented on the merits, arguing that the taxing power may be delegated only to the President, that the alter ego principle is the sole constitutional basis for the secretary's power, that the President's control over the Executive Department cannot be curtailed by Congress, that the Commission's determination is not among the Section 5 conditions, that public interest is indubitably a political question for an official answerable to the people, and that the implementing rules, the Commission's own order and its chairman's statements confirm that its role is merely fact-finding and recommendatory. He added that binding the secretary to a negative determination while letting him reject a positive one was apparently illogical, that his decision should be appealable to the President, and that courts should adopt a hands-off approach to policy, intervening only for blatant illegality or grave abuse of discretion.
